traffic_html:
Is traffic normal today?

US visits so far today, 2026-10-30, counted up to 13:59 Eastern and compared with the same hours on the last 4 Fridays
Traffic is downUS visits are -10% against a normal Friday at this hour (usual swing on a Friday is ±8%). Everything else is -11%, below its usual range. Across the site, 5,167 visits against 5,774 by this hour on a normal Friday (-10%).
US visits5,167-10%vs 5,774 on a normal Friday
every channel, every page, Ashburn and Council Bluffs left out. Usual swing on a Friday is ±8%.
STD city and state pages149-23%vs 195 on a normal Friday, through 09:59
every /std-testing/ city and state page. Usual swing on a Friday is ±36%.
Pages you can buy from389-14%vs 453 on a normal Friday, through 09:59
the /tests/ pages with a cart button, plus the eight /std-testing/ product pages (herpes, HIV, panels). Usual swing on a Friday is ±16%.
Everything else1,995-11%vs 2,238 on a normal Friday, through 09:59
the whole rest of the site. Usual swing on a Friday is ±8%.

Every US visit is counted, from every channel, the same way today and on the earlier days, except visits from Ashburn and Council Bluffs, the datacenter cities, which are left out on both sides. Most of their visits are crawlers: from Sept 8 to Oct 4 they were 11% of US visits but 3% of engaged ones, and they made 8 of the 9 hours that ran above twice their usual. A rise from those two cities alone does not show here. By this hour today 107 visits from them were left out, against 360 on a normal Friday. In hours Analytics has finished sorting, the small share of visits with no page recorded (about 2% on a finished day) is split across the three page groups in proportion to their size, the same way today and on the earlier days. Engaged visits are not used, because Analytics finishes judging which visits were engaged about a day late, so a normal morning looked like a collapse. The cut-off is 13:59 because Analytics keeps adding to recent hours for a while: That hour is the last one whose count stopped changing between two refreshes, and it ended more than 3 hours ago. Comparing a part-day against finished days would show a fake collapse every morning, so only the same hours are counted on both sides.

Monetization livelaunchAug 18 · 12:00 AM

Checkout opened on testing.com. First customer order came through at 1:03 AM from Google organic.

This is the starting line, so there is nothing before it to compare against.

Cart rate since launch

Carts per 1,000 organic visits, split by the section each change affected, with the whole site dashed for reference. Only changes measured on cart rate appear here. Checkout changes move a different number and are judged on their own cards above, and a change to a page people click through to rather than land on gets its own chart below. A section line is the only place a section-level change can show up: STD GEO is about a tenth of our visits, so a big move there barely dents the sitewide line. Carts are the measure rather than orders because orders run single digits a day and cannot separate signal from noise for weeks. 31 days of data so far.

Cart rate on /std-test-pricing/

Share of organic visits to /std-test-pricing/ that add something to the cart. Counted on the page people viewed, not the page they landed on, which is why this is a separate chart and not another line above. Almost nobody arrives on the pricing page from search, they click through to it, so its landing-page numbers run single digits a day while it fires more than half of every cart on the site. One visit counts once here however many tests it adds, so this is a share of people rather than a count of clicks. The two charts count different groups of people and their heights do not compare.

Changes are recorded by hand, big ones only, and each needs the right scope and metric. To add one, edit changes.json.

attribution_html:
Where orders come from

Google Analytics, today so far · treat as directional, not exact
Bot traffic has been removed from every number in this section. Datacenter crawlers from Google Cloud and AWS hit this site hard, loading a page for two seconds and leaving. On 2026-10-30 that was 3,581 of 6,621 US sessions. Visit counts below are engaged sessions, meaning a real person read the page. Google Analytics' own dashboard does not filter this, so its traffic numbers will look several times larger than these and its conversion rates several times worse.
Read this before quoting anything below. These figures come from Google Analytics and are much less reliable than the revenue above. Analytics data runs through 1:14 PM PT, about 1h 40m behind this page. Analytics is also not recording checkout correctly yet: it logged 2 payment steps today against 10 real paid orders, and our purchase event sends no order value, so Analytics reports $0 revenue no matter what sells. Use it to see which pages bring people in, never to count orders or money.

Usual is this page type's cart rate across the last 14 whole days (2026-10-16 to 2026-10-29), with any day the site was not recording carts left out. vs usual only prints a number when today is far enough from usual to mean something. A page type with few carts swings a long way on chance alone, so a small section has to move much further than a big one before it counts. Everything else says normal. Today is still part of a day, so read this as a rate comparison, never as a count. Both rate columns count cart presses rather than people, so a page type where one person adds several tests can read above 100%: the pricing page lists panels side by side and usually does. "Everything else" is every landing page outside the types named above, mostly the category and guide pages, and its usual rate is worked out by subtraction because the history cannot ask for it directly. Direct visits and their carts are left out of every column here, today and usual alike, because a data center that presses the cart button on /tests/ pages dozens of times a day arrives as Direct.

Here it is the share of people who viewed that page and added something to the cart, however they arrived. Above, it is cart presses divided by visits that STARTED on that kind of page. A page can convert people it did not bring in, so a page can rank high here and low there.

Visits above are engaged sessions, meaning someone actually read the page. Today 3,581 of 6,621 US sessions were non-engaged, almost all of it datacenter crawler traffic from Google Cloud and AWS that loads a page for two seconds and leaves. Counting those would roughly quadruple the denominator and make every rate here look four times worse than reality.
